subject: Cerebro Labs — recommended reserved slab and throughput mapping
messages:
From: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>
To: Alan Ross <alan.ross@cerebrolabs.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-04-21T09:12:00-07:00
Subject: Initial slab proposal / questions on peak shape (Cerebro)

Alan —

Thanks again for walking through Cerebro's traffic profile yesterday. Attached is a quick first-pass of capacity math that maps your expected peak token rates to GPU slab sizing. I wanted to surface the assumptions so we can align before I turn this into a formal commitment proposal:

High-level assumptions (please confirm):
- Model variant: 13B quantized (approx equivalent to Llama-2-13B 4-bit).
- Typical output length: 256 tokens per request (median).
- Workload: mix of short-chat (50 tokens) and long responses; we used weighted avg = 256 for sizing.
- Peak sustained target (business-hours): 12,000 tokens/sec.
- Burst capacity target: up to 25,000 tokens/sec for short windows (multi-minute).
- SLO target you asked for: p95 end-to-end latency <= 400 ms for 256-token responses.

Preliminary numbers in the attached sheet (tab: baseline-modeling):
- Baseline per-GPU throughput (A100-80GB, optimized kernels + batching): ~1,200 tokens/sec (batching window ~30–40 ms, effective batch size ~28).
- GPUs for sustained 12k tps: 10 GPUs (12,000 / 1,200).
- Recommended reserved slab (30–40% headroom + maintenance/evacuations): 14 GPUs.
- To cover burst headroom to 25k tps without dropping to on-demand pool, we'd advise a burst policy that allows autoscale to an additional 6 GPUs (or fallback to a compatible model variant).

Tradeoffs we call out in the sheet: lowering batch latency (to get p95 < 300 ms) reduces per-GPU throughput to ~700 tps and increases reserved GPU need to ~18.

Next asks from our side so we can finalize pricing/commit:
1) Confirm peak sustained and burst windows (length / recurrence).
2) Desired p95 and acceptable p99 headroom.
3) Any blackout windows where model updates or evictions are disallowed.

I've attached the throughput workbook and a short SLA scenario PDF. If the assumptions look right, we'll convert the 14-GPU slab into a committed proposal and map to a monthly reserved price.

Best —
Mina Haddad
Senior Solutions Engineer, Redwood Inference

Subject: Re: Initial slab proposal / questions on peak shape (Cerebro)

Mina —

Thanks for the quick turnaround and the workbook. A few clarifications from our side before we lock assumptions:

1) Traffic shape: our current telemetry shows a weekday daytime sustained peak around 09:00–18:00 PDT with a median of ~8k tps and occasional coordinated spikes up to ~22–26k tps for ~3–7 minutes (these are product-driven batch notifications). Weekends are ~35% lower.
2) Latency: our product team prefers p95 <= 350 ms for the majority of interactive flows, but we can tolerate p99 up to 800 ms for non-critical flows. For the notification bursts, sub-second is fine (we just want progress, not timeouts).
3) Model flexibility: we are open to using a slightly smaller/lighter model variant for bursts if it means cost savings, provided answers remain within our accuracy band.

Two asks: can you add a second scenario where batch-window is tightened (latency-first) and show the delta in GPUs + cost? Also can you indicate the live migration/maintenance drain model — we can't afford broad simultaneous evacuations during the morning peak.

I'll loop in procurement once we have committed numbers.

—Alan
Alan Ross
CTO, Cerebro Labs
alan.ross@cerebrolabs.com
From: Mina Haddad <mina_haddad@redwood.com>

Date: 2026-04-21T13:20:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Initial slab proposal / questions on peak shape (Cerebro)

Alan —

Appreciate the detail — that traffic shape aligns nicely with the workbook inputs. I've added a second tab (latency-first) that models a tighter batching policy: target p95 = 320 ms (for 256 tokens). Summary of what changed:

Latency-first scenario:
- Per-GPU throughput drops to ~700 tps (we model reduced batch size ~12–16).
- Sustained 12k tps -> requires ~17 GPUs (12,000 / 700 ≈ 17.1).
- To cover evacuation/maintenance and 20% growth expect to reserve 21 GPUs.

Hybrid approach suggestion (cost/latency balance):
- Reserve a baseline slab of 14 GPUs (latency-balanced).
- Configure policy: during normal interactive traffic use lower-latency profile on 6 GPUs (pin small batches), keep remaining GPUs in throughput-optimized mode. For scheduled burst windows, temporarily relax latency constraints and increase batch depth (or use a lighter model variant) to avoid scaling more than +6 GPUs.

Maintenance / drain model:
- We advise rolling maintenance where no more than 1 GPU per host is drained simultaneously. For the 14-GPU slab that maps to capacity for up to ~2% instantaneous loss without impacting sustained capacity if we keep the 30–40% headroom in place. I documented a step-by-step drain plan in the workbook (tab: operations).

Cost delta (high level):
- Baseline 14-GPU reserved slab: ballpark $93k / month (net of committed discount, exact quote in pricing doc).
- Latency-first 21-GPU reserved slab: ballpark $139k / month.
- Hybrid (14 reserved + short autoscale during bursts): pricing sits between these depending on expected autoscale usage; I can model expected burst-hours to give an average monthly blended cost.

If this sounds reasonable, I'll author the formal proposal and include SLA language (p95, SLO credits) plus a fall-through model variant for burst windows.

Thanks —
Mina

On attachments: added the latency-first scenario and ops drain plan to the workbook.

This is excellent — the hybrid approach is compelling. A couple final operational asks before procurement signs:

1) Can you guarantee no planned maintenance that reduces effective slab capacity by more than 10% during our daytime window (09:00–18:00 PDT)? If you can't guarantee, we'll want a credit schedule in the SLA.
2) For burst-handling: please add a fallback variant (smaller model) decision matrix — which model variant you fallback to and expected QoE delta.

Procurement: once we have the final slab + SLA language we'll run P.O. routing.

—Alan

Alan / team —

Thanks for the clear asks. Mina and I discussed SLA language and fallbacks; summary attached and next steps below.

Quick commitments we can include in the proposal:
- Planned maintenance: we will not schedule capacity-reducing maintenance >10% during your daytime window. Any unavoidable maintenance that impacts capacity >5% will include a customer notice 72 hours prior and will trigger SLA credits per the attached schedule.
- Fallback variant: we recommend '13B-lite-quant' for burst contracts — expected median QoE delta <4% on our internal evals; latency improves ~30% with per-GPU throughput up to ~1,900 tps in burst-optimized mode. Details + evaluation metrics included in the attached PDF.
- Proposal deliverables: formal pricing for a 14-GPU reserved slab, optional autoscale up to +6 GPUs for bursts, and SLA appendix covering p95/p99, maintenance windows, and credits.

Action items:
- Mina: produce the formal commitment doc and SLA appendix (target EOD Thursday).
- Ben: finalize pricing schedule and link to DEAL-2026-0421 in HubSpot.
- Alan / Cerebro: confirm you want the hybrid approach (14 reserved + burst autoscale) or you prefer the latency-first large slab.

Thanks —
